Undermining Climate Action: The Fight by European Oil
Companies against the European Carbon Tax
Fabienne Jouty & Christophe Bonneuil (submitted to to The International History Review)

Abstract: This article examines, in the lead-up to the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio, the role of five major European oil companies—BP in the United Kingdom, Shell in the Netherlands and UK, ENI in Italy, and Total and Elf in France—in scuttling the European Commission’s carbon and energy tax proposal developed within the European institutions since 1989. Based on fresh material from European, national, and private business archives, the study discusses their influence on EC climate policymaking toward a governance tool for regulating CO2 emissions. To this end, we examine the rise of climate change as an issue on the EC political agenda, and within European oil and gas companies. This paper also explores how they cooperated with one another, and worked with several key business associations against any regulation or fiscal instrument for CO 2 reductions. Lastly, this paper assesses the last stages of the battle in 1992, highlighting the arenas in the EC decision-making process that the European oil sector targeted to undermine the carbon tax initiative before the Earth Summit. While most historical research on climate obstruction has focused on US actors, this article is a contribution to the history of climate obstruction in Europe.
Introduction

European oil and gas companies collaborate with each other and with other business organisations?

Since the late 1980s, climate negotiations and policies have sparked fierce battles for influence involving states, business actors, and civil society. Numerous scholarly studies have highlighted the involvement of business actors in European public policy, including shaping such policy, defining key political objectives and agendas, and influencing European integration.3 Researchers have also shed light on the history of oil companies and the strategies used in their response to climate policies on both the global and local level. 1. The rise of the climate within the agenda of the European Community and European oil companies
Scientific knowledge relating to the greenhouse effect dates back to the nineteenth century, with scientific warnings intensifying from the 1950s onward. After garnering some attention between
1965-1972 in the lead-up to the 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm, the
issue remained fairly low-profile in UN arenas until the late 1970s.12 The 1979, the ‘Charney

Report’, commissioned by the American Academy of Sciences, reviewed existing research, estimated 3°C global warming from a doubling of carbon dioxide (CO2) concentrations, and called for action. That same year, the Three Mile Island nuclear accident in the United States brought energy policy to the fore, while the first World Climate Conference held in Geneva led to the launch of the World Climate Research Programme, under the joint sponsorship of the International Council for Science and the World Meteorological Organisation. These and subsequent developments gradually put the climate on the radar of European countries, the European Community (EC), and
European oil and gas companies.

Consequently, by the end of 1989, the three major European institutions had officially recognised the threat of climate change, and the need for a European strategy to address it. Seeking to assert its international influence, the EC aimed, through the issue of the climate, to strengthen intra-European connections, as well as Europe’s voice in international arenas.23 This elicited a response from the
European oil industry, which was directly affected by this emerging policy.
1.2 Threats of climate change: a well-established diagnosis among oil companies

In the 1980s, when climate first entered European policy circles, European oil and gas multinationals such as Elf, Total, ENI, BP, and Shell were aware of ongoing climate change, and were not waiting for academic scientists to enlighten them on the problem. As documented by recent historical research and available internal documents from major oil companies, from the
1960s onwards the oil sector had accumulated considerable knowledge and expertise on global
climate change as a side effect of its products.24

From 1950 to 1972, several avenues of research solidified the hypothesis of anthropogenic global warming.25 In a context of growing environmental awareness, key scientific assessments completed between 1963 and 1972 helped to bring global warming to both US and international attention. At the 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm, three of the 109 final recommendations called for research and vigilance regarding anthropogenic climate change.26

Nobel Prize winner Edward Teller warned—in front of the world’s top oil industry executives as they celebrated the industry’s centennial at Columbia University—of climate warming and the human consequences of rising oceans. A few years later, a 1965 report submitted to the White

1.3. Sharing climate expertise internally, relativising it externally

When it became clear in the early 1980s that climate change would become an issue at both national and international level, oil companies not only developed climate research and intelligence for themselves (forecasting the intensity of global warming, developing greener technologies and products, and monitoring environmental policy proposals and processes were potential competitive advantages), but they also began to share their knowledge and strategies in order to better address policy proposals for controlling emissions and taxing fossil fuels. Beyond the US-centred API, a key arena for more international circulations within the oil sector was the International Petroleum
Industry Environmental Conservation Association (IPIECA, an oil sector business organisation established in 1974 as a stakeholder in the UN Environment Programme). At an IPIECA meeting in
Texas in 1984, ‘the Exxon people gave us a heads-up’ on climate science, recalled the

Environmental Director for the French oil company Elf at the time.42 It was thanks to this collective learning effort within the confines of IPIECA that Elf’s (confidential) annual environmental report for 1985 warned that ‘the accumulation of CO2 and CH4 in the atmosphere and the resulting greenhouse effect will inevitably modify our environment. All models are unanimous in predicting global warming’. The report also alerted senior management of proposed fiscal policy instruments that would be detrimental to the company: ‘The first reactions have been, of course, to “tax fossil fuels”, so it is obvious that the oil industry will once again have to prepare to defend itself’.43

2. Preparing to undermine EC climate policy, 1989-1991
2.1. The rise of a fiscal instrument in EEC arenas to address greenhouse gases
The first steps towards European climate strategy were taken in December 1988, when the Rhodes

Environment Council urged the Commission and member states ‘to play their full part in defining and implementing a global response to this problem’.45 In June 1989, the Environment Council called for measures promoting non-fossil energy sources, as well as concrete proposals for CO2 reductions. The Noordwijk Conference, which was held by the Dutch government in close collaboration with France and Norway on 6-7 November 1989, sought a binding agreement on CO₂ emissions. However, it failed because four delegations out of the 68 countries represented—the

United States, Japan, the Soviet Union, and the United Kingdom—refused to make an agreement on reducing emissions.46 This led to greater emphasis on tax instruments to overcome the stalemate on targets, as well as calls for the EEC to take the lead in helping to change US positions. On 28
November 1989, the Environment Council, chaired by the French Minister Brice Lalonde, stated:

Fiscal instruments can play an important role in changing the behaviour of economic actors in order to reduce environmental damage. The Council invites the Commission to study, with the help of the competent national experts, the use of economic and fiscal instruments in the Community to preserve the environment and to present its conclusions to the competent bodies.47

As its promoters suggested, an ecotax, or an environmental tax on fossil fuels, was a gentler and more flexible instrument, with an educational component as well. Set initially at a very low rate and gradually increased, it would encourage more environmentally-friendly behaviour by imposing additional costs on activities or products with a negative environmental impact. While some authors attributed the UK’s strong opposition to the EC carbon and energy tax proposal to the careful avoidance of new taxes during the sensitive period of coal mine closures,121 our research as well as the findings of Daley et al. suggest a close relationship between the UK government and corporations since the mid-1980s. This ensured that business, including the oil sector, played a role in shaping the UK’s position on European climate policy.122
In the Netherlands, Shell’s relationship with the Social Democratic government was less than harmonious. As early as 1990, the country supported the European climate strategy and adopted a
‘small (revenue-raising) carbon tax’,123 as did Finland in 1990, Sweden in 1991, and Denmark in
1993. Despite Shell’s internal memo from 1988 on ‘The Greenhouse Effect’ mentioned above,

which warned of the impact of climate change, in 1989 Shell began funding Frits Böttcher, a prominent Dutch climate change denier, and joined the GCC, a hardline opponent of policies reducing greenhouse gas emissions.124 Lodewijk van Wachem himself, Shell’s CEO since the 1980s, implemented a strategy of sowing doubt, claiming in 1992 that although ‘the political world strongly supports the view that human-induced emissions are likely to increase the greenhouse effect’, there was still a debate about ‘fundamental science’ with respect to the effects of climate change ‘in different regions of the world’. He argued that ‘government intervention in the change process, whether at the national or international level, should not distort competitive forces’, emphasising that the industry’s ability to ‘fund programs reducing its environmental impact depends on its continued profitability’. He believed that ‘a technical solution will be found for almost all environmental problems’.125

Germany had supported a carbon tax since 1989, although its backing became increasingly hesitant and discreet as 1992 progressed. The country had no major oil company headquartered in its territory, but coal interests and energy-intensive industries were very powerful. As a result, by late
1991, the government demanded that the tax should include transitional and exclusionary measures
for coal.126

Conclusion

Despite the initial intention to go to the 1992 Earth Summit with ambitious targets and measures addressing climate change—thereby presenting an exemplary environmental strategy for other countries—the European Commission withdrew its carbon tax plan on the eve of the summit, leaving member states deeply divided. Without an Environment Commissioner at the Rio Summit,

Europe was unable to take on the leadership role it had aspired to, failing to push for anything more ambitious than a framework convention lacking a timeline, targets, and commitments.
This paper opened with the boasts of a close advisor to the CEO of Elf, proudly ascribing the defeat of the ecotax to Elf’s lobbying efforts. As this paper has demonstrated, it was actually several

European oil companies that clearly strove to sink the ecotax, collaborating to share information, rhetoric, and strategies. Determining the oil industry’s exact impact in the battle over carbon taxation is challenging, because it was not the only sector fighting for a non-tax-based alternative, and the struggle unfolded across multiple fronts, including negotiations within the INC, opposition from to a carbon tax on the part of certain OECD members such as the United States, and backlash from OPEC. Navigating the intricacies of this multi-arena, multi-stakeholder landscape, aided by a wealth of printed and archival resources, this article has documented the intense lobbying efforts deployed by the European oil industry to prevent the adoption of a European carbon tax before the
Rio Summit.

It firstly showed how Elf, ENI, BP, Shell, and Total had fairly up-to-date knowledge of the greenhouse effect and its potential impact well before the problem became an EC policy issue in the late 1980s. Second, our study documented how they exchanged information, shared scientific, technical, and economic expertise relating to climate change and emerging climate regulations, drafted common arguments, and elaborated joint strategies. IPIECA and EUROPIA served as key arenas for inter-firm cooperation across the oil sector. Archival documents and interviews shed light on IPIECA’s key role as a channel for transferring a ‘merchant of doubt strategy’ from the US to

Europe. Endowed with authoritative cross-sectoral business authority, the ICC and UNICE became strategic organizations to participate in for oil companies, in order to align them with their own obstruction strategy. These channels for collaboration facilitated the rapid spread of arguments and strategies for public relations. They also streamlined the oil sector’s simultaneous efforts across three main battlegrounds: i) international arenas (far beyond Europe’s boundaries); ii) the offices and corridors of Brussels (to leverage differences between Commissioners and DGs); and iii)
national governments (to change the positions of key member states).

Ultimately, while these five companies pursued a shared goal, there were differences in their strategies, tactical repertoire, and discourses. Based on the sources we were able to access, it appears that from 1989 to 1992, Shell was more radically inclined towards promoting the denial of anthropogenic climate change, while ENI adopted a somewhat more moderate approach, and BP,
Elf, and Total occupied a middle ground with regard to sowing doubt.
